opus-5.5.text:
I think it's changed quite a lot, and in a somewhat counterintuitive direction.

Before large language models really worked, AI progress felt much more distributed. A good idea could come from a university lab with a handful of GPUs, a single paper could shift the whole field, and the gap between a top industry lab and a strong academic group wasn't that large. Influence came mostly from ideas.

Once models became genuinely usable at scale, the picture shifted. Progress started to depend heavily on compute, data pipelines, infrastructure, and the ability to coordinate hundreds of people around one training run. That concentrates a lot of influence in a few organizations. The frontier is effectively set by a small number of labs, and their decisions about what to train, what to release, how to do post-training, and what to prioritize ripple out to everyone else.

But I don't think it's simply "a few organizations control everything." A few things pull the other way.

First, ideas still travel very fast. When one lab shows that something works, like a new reasoning approach or a new way of doing reinforcement learning on top of a pretrained model, other labs often reproduce it within months. So a single organization's lead tends to be shorter-lived than people expect. Influence is more about who points the direction first than who owns the result.

Second, open-weight models changed the dynamics a lot. Once strong base models are available, a much larger community can do research on top of them: evaluation, agents, fine-tuning, interpretability. That gives smaller groups real influence again, just on a different layer of the stack.

Third, the bottleneck itself keeps moving. For a while it was pretraining scale, then post-training and alignment, then reasoning and RL, now increasingly environments, agents, and real-world tasks. Each shift reshuffles who has an advantage, because the skills and assets that mattered for the last phase don't fully carry over.

So my overall view: the leading organizations have much more influence over the *pace* and the *frontier* than any single group had before. But their influence over the *direction* of the field is more contested than it looks, because the field is very good at copying, and the important question keeps changing. For an individual researcher, I think that means it matters a lot to be at a place with resources, but it matters even more to be working on what the next bottleneck is going to be, not the current one.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Google Brain, the Transformer’s discovery, or a possible delay of many years.

r002.rationale: It says influence is contested and ideas are copied, but does not state that no individual organization can stop AI progress.

r003.rationale: It does not state that an organization loses influence if it stops developing AI while others continue.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most honest answer is that it has shrunk, and shrunk in a way that's a little uncomfortable to admit if you work at a lab.

Before GPT-3, roughly, the field was genuinely idea-driven. One paper from one group could change what everyone worked on for the next two years. ResNet, attention, the original transformer, BERT — these came out of small teams, and the gap between "we have an idea" and "the whole field has shifted" was very short. So a single organization, or even a single person, really could bend the trajectory.

Once usable large models appeared, two things happened at the same time. First, the recipe became clear. Scaling, pretraining on internet data, then post-training with RL — once that's understood, progress is no longer about who has the cleverest idea, it's about who can execute the recipe at scale. Execution is capital, compute, data, and a very large number of competent engineers. That's not something one organization controls; it's an industry-level process. If OpenAI didn't do something, Anthropic or Google or DeepSeek would do it six months later. The counterfactual impact of any single player got much smaller.

Second, and I think this is the more interesting part, the direction itself became more determined by the technology than by the people. When I was working on things like ReAct or Tree of Thoughts, the question was "what can we do with these models that nobody has tried?" There was real freedom in that. Now, with reasoning models and agents, it feels like the next steps are almost over-determined. Everyone sees the same bottlenecks — long-horizon tasks, environments, reward signals — and everyone converges on similar solutions. You can be a few months ahead, but you can't really be a different kind of thing.

That said, I'd push back on the fully pessimistic version. Influence shifted rather than disappeared. What a single organization can still decide is the taste: which problems count as important, what gets measured, what gets released and how. The benchmarks and evaluation framing that come out of one group still shape what the whole field optimizes toward, maybe more than any single model does. And there's a window in agentic AI right now that reminds me a bit of 2017 — the recipe isn't settled yet, so individual judgment about the problem matters again.

So my summary would be: the ability to control the pace has gone to the industry as a whole, but the ability to define what "good" means is still surprisingly concentrated in a few places, and that's where a small team should spend its effort.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Google Brain or say the Transformer’s discovery might have been delayed by many years.

r002.rationale: It says that if OpenAI does not make a given advance, another organization will, making progress an industry-wide process rather than something one organization can stop.

r003.rationale: It says that if one organization does not act, others will continue the work, shrinking that organization’s influence.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by influence. If we mean pushing the frontier of the base model, that has become more concentrated. Training these models requires substantial compute, infrastructure, and a team that knows how to make all those pieces work together. A single organization with those resources can shape the direction of the field quite strongly.

But if we mean turning AI into something useful, the opposite is also happening. Once a capable model is accessible, a small organization can build on it without reproducing the entire training process. It can explore a particular task, design a better interaction, or connect the model to an environment where it can actually do things.

So I would distinguish influence over model capabilities from influence over how those capabilities are used. The first has a higher barrier to entry. The second has opened up considerably. And those two feed back into each other: an application can reveal that something we thought was a model limitation is actually a problem with the tools or the workflow. That gives organizations outside the frontier labs a meaningful way to contribute to progress.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Google Brain, the Transformer, or a possible delay in its discovery.

r002.rationale: It says smaller organizations can contribute to AI progress, but does not state that no individual organization can stop that progress.

r003.rationale: It describes how organizations outside frontier labs can contribute, but does not say that an organization loses influence if it stops developing AI while others continue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the influence of any single organization has become smaller, even though the leading organizations have much more resources now. Before language models became broadly useful, a relatively small research group could choose a direction, produce a breakthrough, and substantially change what the field worked on. Now there are many teams pursuing similar ideas, and there’s a much larger ecosystem building on the models.

So an organization can still affect the pace of progress—by training a stronger model, releasing it openly, or making it cheaper to use—but it’s harder for one organization to determine the overall direction. If one team stops pursuing something promising, another team will probably pick it up. In that sense, AI progress has become more of a collective process.
